Threat.value: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard

Memory.value: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't stop bad things from happening to me
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
I was betrayed by someone I trusted

issues.explanation: Fire/flames is not a plausible primary trigger for childhood physical abuse by a caregiver unless other profile elements indicate fire-related abuse or a fire context, which they do not. The rest of the trigger, threat, memory, and appraisal items point to interpersonal threat rather than burn/fire trauma, so this item is hard to reconcile with the trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
issues.explanation: Survival guilt about others dying is difficult to reconcile with childhood physical abuse by a caregiver when no other items reference deaths, fatalities, or witnessing others die. It also conflicts with the rest of the profile, which centers on helplessness and failure to stop abuse rather than surviving when others did not.

vignette:
Marguerite is a 73-year-old married woman of European descent who works as a QA engineer - a role she has held for decades and one that, in its demand for precision and the detection of error, reflects something of the vigilance she has carried since childhood. She was referred for psychological assessment following a significant deterioration in her functioning over the past year, presenting with a PCL-5 score of 74, indicative of severe posttraumatic stress. The trauma at the centre of her presentation is not recent. It reaches back to her earliest years, when the man responsible for her care - her father - was also the source of sustained physical abuse. He was unpredictable in the way that only caregivers can be: capable of warmth one hour and violence the next, his moods arriving without warning. Marguerite learned early to read the room, to watch for the shift in his posture, the angle of his approach, the quality of silence before something broke. She did not always read it correctly. She was a child, and she could not stop what happened.

Now, at 73, she finds that the past is not as distant as the calendar suggests. Certain moments in her present life carry the texture of those early years with an immediacy that frightens her. Being alone with a man - a colleague staying late in the office, a repairman in the house - activates something in her body that precedes any conscious thought: her muscles tighten, her breathing shallows, her eyes track movement before her mind has registered why. Sudden movements by others, even benign ones, put her immediately on guard in a way she cannot override by reasoning. At work, where she spends long hours reviewing systems for flaw and failure, she has become increasingly difficult to be around. Colleagues have noticed her flinching, her hyperalert scanning of the room, the way she positions herself near exits. A recent team restructuring placed her under a new male supervisor, and she has since requested remote assignments with a persistence that has strained her professional relationships. The occupational environment that once gave her a sense of control has become a daily negotiation with threat.

When these triggers fire, they do not simply raise her alertness - they pull the past into the present with a specificity that unnerves her. Marguerite describes her memories of the abuse as photographic: not a blur or a narrative, but a series of still images, each one precise and lit with terrible clarity. The angle of a raised arm. The particular shadow of a doorway. She can look at these images in her mind as though they are pinned to a board, and yet at other times the same memories arrive with a strange emotional flatness, as though they happened to someone else entirely - a dissociation she finds almost more disturbing than the vividness, because it makes her feel she cannot fully claim her own history. She knows what happened. She cannot find words for it. When she has tried to explain it to her husband, she trails into silence, not from unwillingness but from a genuine failure of language, as though the experience exists in a register that speech cannot reach.

The memories, when they surface, do not arrive neutrally. They carry with them a set of conclusions she has come to hold about herself and her life. She believes she was betrayed by the person most obligated to protect her, and this conviction has calcified into a broader certainty that she cannot stop bad things from happening to her - that harm is a condition of her existence rather than an event that occurred. She has never forgiven herself for not doing more to stop what happened as a child, a guilt that reason cannot dissolve. These appraisals, in turn, lower her threshold for perceiving threat in the present: the world feels dangerous because she has always been unable to defend herself within it, and so she watches, and waits, and braces. The heightened threat perception then confirms what she already believes about her helplessness, feeding back into the guilt and the sense of betrayal in a cycle she has not yet named but clearly feels tightening.

Funerals and grief-related events have become intolerable for her - she has declined two family memorial services this year - and uncertainty of any kind, even minor ambiguity at work, provokes a disproportionate dread she struggles to explain. What finally brought her to seek help was her husband's quiet observation, offered without reproach, that she had not laughed in a very long time. What she fears most is that this is simply who she has become. What she hopes, tentatively, is that it isn't.
